blocks.content: Start this standalone lab from **Dashboards** to build and save a synthetic signal snapshot.

blocks.tooltip: Move to the workspace for the next part of this lab.
blocks.content: Open **Dashboards** to begin.
Prepare **TestData** if it is missing; an existing source completes this section automatically, while creating one requires admin access on Cloud or OSS.

blocks.tooltip: Prepare a synthetic source only when one is missing.
blocks.content: Open **Add data source**.

blocks.tooltip: No external credentials are needed for this practice data.
blocks.content: Search for **TestData**.

blocks.tooltip: Create a local source of synthetic samples.
blocks.content: Click **TestData** to create the data source.
You have a reusable synthetic data source that needs no external service or credentials.

whenTrue.prompt: Select your TestData source; its name may differ in your organization.

blocks.content: Create a fresh dashboard and configure a **Stat** panel using your chosen practice source.

blocks.tooltip: Move to the workspace for the next part of this lab.
blocks.content: Create a fresh dashboard for this lab.
Open **Add** to show the controls for creating a panel.
blocks.tooltip: Show the controls for adding dashboard elements.
Make space for a synthetic signal.
blocks.content: Click **Panel** to add a panel.

blocks.tooltip: Configure how the data will be presented.
blocks.content: Click **Edit visualization** to open the panel editor.

blocks.tooltip: Use the source chosen earlier even if its name differs.
blocks.content: In the data source picker, select {{practiceSource}}.
Choose **Stat** as the visualization.

steps.tooltip: Choose how to represent the signal.
Summarize the signal as a prominent number.

blocks.tooltip: Make this result easy to recognize later.
blocks.content: Under **Panel options**, set **Title** to `Signal snapshot`.
You have a named panel connected to your practice source.
Bound one random walk between 0 and 100, starting at 50, to make visual changes easier to interpret.

blocks.tooltip: Prevent generated values from falling below zero.
blocks.content: In query **A**, set **Min** to `0`.

blocks.tooltip: Keep generated values within the practice range.
blocks.content: In query **A**, set **Max** to `100`.

blocks.tooltip: Begin the synthetic walk halfway through its bounds.
blocks.content: In query **A**, set **Start value** to `50`.

blocks.tooltip: Generate practice readings with the configured bounds.
blocks.content: Run the query to display the practice signal.
You have generated one bounded synthetic signal for the visualization exercises.
Compare individual samples with a summary: **All values** displays separate readings, while **Calculate** combines them into one value per signal; you will use **Mean** to average the readings.

blocks.tooltip: Inspect individual samples before selecting a summary.
blocks.content: Under **Value options**, set **Show** to **All values** to display individual samples.

blocks.tooltip: Keep the individual sample preview manageable.
blocks.content: Under **Value options**, set **Limit** to `5` to display up to five samples.

blocks.tooltip: Reduce each signal to one summary.
blocks.content: Under **Value options**, set **Show** to **Calculate** to display one summary per signal.

blocks.tooltip: Average the values in the displayed time range.
blocks.content: Under **Value options**, set **Calculation** to **Mean** to average the samples returned for the displayed time range.

blocks.tooltip: Use consistent precision for an easy-to-read result.
blocks.content: Under **Standard options**, set **Decimals** to `1`.

blocks.tooltip: Make the synthetic nature of the number explicit.
blocks.content: Under **Standard options**, set **Display name** to `Practice signal`.
Your main number is now the average of the returned samples across the displayed time range, rather than just the last sample; the five-value preview limit does not limit this calculation.

blocks.question: What does the configured mean summarize?

choices.text: Values across the displayed time range.
choices.hint: The mean is an average across the displayed time range, not the last reading.

choices.text: Only the final sample in the time range.
choices.hint: The mean is an average across the displayed time range, not the last reading.

blocks.content: Add a label, sparkline, and background color so the average has context: samples of 10, 50, and 90 average 50, but the sparkline reveals their rise.

blocks.tooltip: Keep identifying context beside the summary.
blocks.content: Under **Stat styles**, set **Text mode** to **Value and name** to label the summary.

blocks.tooltip: Expose variation that an average alone can hide.
blocks.content: Under **Stat styles**, set **Graph mode** to **Area** to see how samples vary over time.

blocks.tooltip: Carry the level-based color through the card background.
blocks.content: Under **Stat styles**, set **Color mode** to **Background Gradient** to color the background using the calculated mean.
The sparkline shows variation hidden by the average, while the background color represents the calculated mean.
Set a threshold for the mean and compare it with percent change: a first sample of 50 and last sample of 60 gives (60 − 50) / 50 × 100 = 20%, regardless of the samples between them.

blocks.tooltip: Use 70 as an illustrative color boundary without creating an alert.
blocks.content: Under **Thresholds**, set the existing threshold value to `70`; the mean now determines which threshold color fills the background, without creating an alert.

blocks.tooltip: Add first-to-last movement as context for the average.
blocks.content: Under **Stat styles**, enable **Show percent change** to compare the first and last samples rather than the mean.

blocks.reftarget: {grafana:components.PanelEditor.OptionsPane.fieldLabel:Stat styles Percent change color mode} input
blocks.tooltip: Treat a decrease as favorable in this practice scenario.
blocks.content: Under **Stat styles**, set **Percent change color mode** to **Inverted**: decreases appear green and increases red for this lower-is-better example.

blocks.tooltip: Interpret level, variation, and change together without inferring real service health.
blocks.content: Compare the mean, sparkline, and percent change: the mean summarizes all samples, the sparkline shows their path, and percent change compares the endpoints. A low mean can coexist with a rising last sample.
Inverted coloring changes only the interpretation of the percent-change indicator: a decrease is green and an increase red, while the data, calculation, and mean-based threshold color stay unchanged.

blocks.question: Why use inverted percent-change coloring in this exercise?

choices.text: A decrease is favorable in the lower-is-better scenario.
choices.hint: Coloring expresses desirability; it does not change the data.

choices.text: It changes the underlying synthetic readings.
choices.hint: Coloring expresses desirability; it does not change the data.

blocks.content: Save your dashboard and inspect the finished signal snapshot.

blocks.tooltip: Keep the panel settings while returning to the larger workspace.
blocks.content: Click **Back** to return to the dashboard.
Save the dashboard as Stat lab - Signal snapshot.

steps.tooltip: Persist the work through one uninterrupted drawer sequence.
steps.description: Click **Save** to open the save drawer.

steps.tooltip: Give the saved result a recognizable name.
steps.description: Enter Stat lab - Signal snapshot as the dashboard title.

blocks.tooltip: Check the visible result after persistence without changing its configuration.
blocks.content: Confirm that Stat lab - Signal snapshot is saved and that Signal snapshot displays Practice signal with a one-decimal mean, an area sparkline, a gradient background, and percent change; the configuration uses a threshold at 70 and inverted change coloring, while the generated readings can vary.
You have learned to save the finished configuration and confirm its visible result on the dashboard.
